replying_to: Replying to Statistically Undetectable Backdoors in Deep Neural Networks
display_title: Official Review of Submission20344 by Reviewer GBDa

summary.value: The paper discusses a method for planting a backdoor into neural networks that is statistically undetectable. The main idea involves a random compression embedding layer right after the input. This layer is created by rejection sampling in such a way that a given fixed perturbation vector z, when added to any input x, will result in a very small difference in the output. At the same time, this vector cannot be efficiently identified if only the weights of the embedding layer are known. The construction is supported by an extensive theoretical analysis that establishes strong cryptographic properties.

strengths.value: The paper provides thorough theoretical support regarding the cryptographic properties and the indistinguishability of the backdoored random compression layer, which might potentially help establish cryptographic applications in neural networks.

weaknesses.value:
The paper heavily builds on the reference Bogdanov et al (2025), where most of the key ideas have already been established, most importantly, the secure hash-like properties of the Gaussian embedding layer included in the proposed construction. The paper does offer novelty, though, regarding the total variation distance of the plain and backdoored layer and the backdoor strength.

However, the paper poses assumptions that, in the present form, almost prevent any meaningful applications of the idea. A random compression layer at the beginning is highly unusual. While one can argue that it is a theoretically justified technique for feature extraction, in current architectures it is  not applied, and if its sole purpose is to carry backdoors, then users will simply avoid such networks.  The Lipschitz assumption in the remaining part of the network is extremely strong, and it is certainly not practical.

The theoretical results are very interesting but in general, the proposed application is not necessarily the best for them. In other cryptographic tasks, like a steganographic signature of the model weights to prevent model theft, they would work much better. In that case, even the Lipschitz assumption is unnecessary. The "backdoors" that are proposed are not really backdoors in the usual sense, as they are unsuitable to controllably change model outputs. The vector z is more like a signature of the model.

questions.value:
Can you summarize the contributions relative to Bogdanov et al 2025?

Can you use this technique to "backdoor" neural networks in the usual sense of maliciously and controllably changing the network outcome by manipulating the input?

While the vector z cannot be recovered, one can get suspicious by looking at the unusual model architecture. Can you hide the technique in existing architectures?

What is your idea about other applications, like watermarking? Wouldn't that be much more suitable? If not, why? How about related work in that area?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission20344 by Reviewer GBDa

comment.value:
Thank you for your thoughtful review. We’re glad that you found the theoretical support for our construction thorough. We respond to your review below, and we hope that our response adequately addresses your questions and concerns. If not, please let us know so that we can appropriately respond. We have also uploaded a **revision** of our paper that includes a section that addresses one of your comments on other possible applications like watermarking; see Section 1.2 in the revision.

**Contributions compared to Bogdanov et al. (2025)**:

Bogdanov et al. (2025) focused on the computational complexity of finding contracting discrete vectors in random linear maps. The main difference between our works is that they do not consider any “backdooring” algorithm for outputting matrices with certain properties. They do not ask what asymmetry of power can arise between efficient parties when a random compression matrix could be backdoored. Much of the technical work in our submission is an efficient algorithm for planting a solution $\mathbf{z}$ in a random compressing matrix $\mathbf{A}$ exactly for such a power asymmetry, with a lot of effort spent in the analysis. Appendix B gives the full analysis, none of which is relevant to or present in Bogdanov et al. (2025). The perspective on using random compressing maps as a source for backdoors in neural networks does not show up anywhere in Bogdanov et al. (2025), and our preliminary empirical findings have no analog in Bogdanov et al. (2025).

One smaller point is that they considered how well the output embedding distances preserve the input distances. Our focus is slightly different in that we do not consider output distance as compared to the input distance; we simply try to understand when output distance can be made small for any two distinct discrete inputs.

**Use of our backdoors**:

Below, we present a scenario in which the backdoor notion we construct is significant and potentially worrisome. Imagine that one trains a DNN as an image embedding model used within a facial recognition system. Let $M$ denote the model given as a DNN. To recognize a new image $\mathbf{x}$, one would evaluate $M(\mathbf{x})$ and compute the distances between $M(\mathbf{x})$ and $M(\mathbf{x}’)$ for target images $\mathbf{x}’$ and apply a threshold. If there is an existing target image $\mathbf{x}’$ such that $\| M(\mathbf{x}) - M(\mathbf{x}’) \|$ is sufficiently small, there is a “match” and the system recognizes the image.

Our backdoor notion in this setting would mean the following. With the backdoor, one can take any image and generate a fake, different image that is a “fake match” with the original image according to this recognition system. Conversely, without the backdoor, no one else has this ability to “fool” the recognition system, even for one image.

**Model architecture concerns**:

It is true that if no one were to use such a model architecture *except* when planting backdoors, then a user could indeed be suspicious upon seeing the model. Our view is that the combination of Constraints 1, 2, and 3 is not a priori unreasonable for a DNN, as we justify in Section 1.1. Whether current state-of-the-art models satisfy these constraints or not is an independent question and is not the focus of our motivation.

That being said, if still unsatisfied with these constraints, one can view our result as a proof of concept, where strong, cryptographic reasoning gives provable power asymmetries. A more direct interpretation of our result is that there is an efficient way to backdoor the *JL embedding itself*, irrespective of subsequent layers. We believe that this perspective is illuminating in its own right, independently of any extension to DNNs or current architectures.

Furthermore, many of the constraints in our architecture can be relaxed if we no longer require provable limits on what users can do *without* the backdoor. For example, we would have the flexibility of no longer requiring the model to be bilipschitz after the first layer; lipschitzness itself suffices. This means that we can use standard ReLUs (and variants like GELU) instead of Leaky ReLUs. It also means that we can handle compressing matrices, so we can handle models that have scalar outputs (instead of high-dimensional embeddings). We also would not need to limit ourselves to discrete inputs.

**Watermarking & other applications**:

We thank you for bringing up the notion of watermarking. In the introduction, we briefly mentioned a “positive use” of our backdoors, which could be used as an authentication mechanism to establish model provenance / ownership. Indeed, this directly follows from our backdoor definition; any colliding adversarial example directly proves “ownership”, in the sense of proof of sampling the matrix $\mathbf{A}$. In our revision, Section 1.2 elaborates on this point, but if there are any particular questions about this application that you have, please let us know.

summary.value: The authors present a strategy to train DNNs with statistically undetectable backdoors, empowering model trainers with more control to tamper with the training process without model users' knowledge. Both theoretical justifications and empirical studies are presented.

strengths.value:
The presented study is very interesting. 

Both theoretical and empirical justifications are convincing.

weaknesses.value: The nature of the backdoors needs future clarification.

questions.value:
The computed backdoors appear to be model-dependent. Given a set of data D, 
1. An algorithm A and its backdoored version B output DNNs M_A and M_B, computing a backdoor z for a given x. Suppose another algorithm A', trained on a dataset following the same distribution as D, outputs M_A'. Will z be able to fool M_A' ? 
2. If a random noise dz is added to z, will M_A and its backdoored counterpart M_B output indistinguishable results with  x+z+dz  as the input? 

Both questions are concerned with the generality of the computed backdoors. If their adversity is dependent on a specific algorithm, it's unclear how much practical use this discovery can offer. 
 
Minor comments:

On page 3, "than" ---> then

On page 7, "a the same pair " ---> remove "a"

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission20344 by Reviewer SidL

comment.value:
Thank you for your positive review. We’re glad that you found the study interesting and our theoretical and empirical justifications convincing. We respond to your review below, and we hope that our response adequately addresses your questions and concerns. If not, please let us know so that we can appropriately respond. We have also uploaded a **revision** of our paper that corrects the minor comments you pointed out and includes a new section (Section 1.2) on another perspective of our result for proving model *provenance* or *ownership*. 

**Answer to Question #1**:

The backdoor z depends on the randomness used during training, and it is independent of the set of data D. If an adversary has control over training for both M_A and M_A’, it can ensure that z fools both of them. However, if an adversary has no control over the training of one of them, say M_A’, then z would not fool M_A’. To summarize, our backdooring mechanism does not tamper with the set of data D, but rather with the random bits used during training. 

**Answer to Question #2**:

In our result, M_A and M_B are close in total variation distance, meaning that there does not exist *any* test that distinguishes them with noticeable probability. In particular, their input/output behavior as functions will be statistically close. One thing worth clarifying is that the notion of the vector z in M_A would be implicit, since there is no clear choice of a backdoor vector z in the “honest” model M_A (as M_A is not backdoored).

**Generality of the backdoors**:

We emphasize that our backdoors apply to all DNN training algorithms that are subject to Constraints 1, 2, and 3. It does not depend on which specific algorithm is used. More precisely, our construction takes *any* DNN training algorithm (subject to the constraints) and modifies the algorithm (just in how it samples the first layer matrix A) to create a backdoored model.

**Typos**:

Finally, we thank you for catching and pointing out our typos. We greatly appreciate it, and we corrected them in our revision.

comment.value:
Thank you for your follow up. We want to ensure that we are understanding your question correctly. We see two possible interpretations of it, both of which we address below. If neither of these interpretations is what you mean, please let us know and we can clarify further.

**Interpretation A**: *Is it too strong and impractical to assume that the adversary has control over all DNNs produced at large?*

We do not assume this. We view our backdoors as meaningful even if there are some models M_A that are backdoored and some models M_A’ that are not; the backdoors need not be deployed unilaterally and globally to be notable. For example, in the context of delegating the task of training a neural network, maybe one of the service providers is malicious, even if other providers are not; it could still impact all of that service provider’s users. Even the ability to selectively target one specific user is worthy of rigorous study, in our view. In fact, if one were to view our backdoor as a proof of model provenance (see Section 1.2 in the revision), our backdooring algorithm can be viewed in a positive way that is available for adoption by model trainers, whether it be one or many.

That being said, there could be instances in which backdoored algorithms indeed *are* deployed at large. Randomness generation is a complex and subtle task, and as such, it is often delegated to particular libraries or secure hardware implementations. For example, I would imagine most practitioners trust that the function “numpy.random.normal()” outputs a clean Gaussian sample without any adversarial auxiliary information. If a malicious party were to implement this function in a way that gives them access to a backdoor (as in our paper), then they could perhaps have broad access to backdoors in DNNs. While such threats may seem hypothetical at first glance, in cryptography standardization, there have been famous and devastating instances of malicious randomness generation. For example, the Dual_EC_DRBG algorithm is a pseudorandom number generator that was standardized by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in the USA, but it was later discovered that the National Security Agency (NSA) planted a secret backdoor in it.

**Interpretation B**: *Is it too strong and impractical of a threat model to assume that an adversary has access to a whole model M_A, instead of just one specific component of the model?*

The adversary needs to change only how the first layer of the model is sampled (just the randomness). All other components of the model can be generated and trained in the exact same way as it would be normally.

display_title: Official Review of Submission20344 by Reviewer hA7G

summary.value: This paper proposes a method for planting statistically undetectable backdoors into certain deep neural networks, showing that there's a significant power imbalance between the model's creator and its users: even with full white-box access, a user cannot detect the existence of a backdoor, which allows the creator to generate invariance-based adversarial examples, nor can it create such examples itself. This means the creator can use a secret key ($z$) to make any input $x$ and a distant, altered input $x'$ (e.g., $x+z$) produce nearly identical outputs. Under standard cryptographic assumptions, it is provably impossible for a user without the key to find such colliding pairs. The technique applies to feedforward DNNs where the first layer is a frozen, compressing Gaussian matrix and all subsequent layers are bi-Lipschitz. The backdoor is embedded by specially generating this first-layer matrix, conditioned on the secret vector $z$ (which is also drawn at random first).

strengths.value:
- The paper studies an important topic both for theoreticians and practitioners.

- The guarantees are rather strong, since they hold even when one has white-box access to the model.

- The technical constructions are using some interesting ideas.

- The exposition is pretty clean and nice to read.

weaknesses.value:
- Set of models is a bit restrictive and makes the technical result less interesting than I originally thought after reading the abstract; essentially all the difficulty of handling the DNN comes from the first layer because of the Lipschitzness condition of the subsequent layers. Could you comment on if you see a technical path towards extending the results to more general families of DNNs?

- I'm a bit confused about the notion of backdoor here: prior work asks for the ability of the model creator to map input examples to ones that are close, and their labels are far. This paper adopts a dual notion: it asks for input examples that are far but their labels are close. Moreover, the formal definition of this notion of backdoors requires that the model creator can produce a single pair of "collisions."

Why did use this notion over the more well-studied one? Intuitively, the former requirement of the backdoor (the one studied in prior work) sounds more reasonable. Could you explain why you chose this notion of backdoors, how it compares with the one I'm suggesting here, and if you can handle this notion?

Despite these concerns, I think that the result is interesting in its own right, so I'm on the positive side. However, it is important to clarify why these colliding inputs should be thought of as backdoors (given the extensive prior work), and if there isn't a good justification to do so it would be good to phrase the results differently.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission20344 by Reviewer hA7G

comment.value:
Thank you for your positive review. We’re glad that you appreciated our clean exposition and the strong guarantees in our result. We respond to your review below, and we hope that our response adequately addresses your questions and concerns. If not, please let us know so that we can appropriately respond. We have also uploaded a **revision** of our paper that includes a new section (Section 1.2) on another perspective of our result for proving model *provenance* or *ownership*. 

**More general families of DNNs**:

We believe that understanding how to extend our result to a larger family of DNNs is a fascinating future research direction. Below, we mention two possible approaches, but it is a question that we are actively investigating as follow-up.

*1.* Many of the constraints in our architecture can be relaxed if we no longer require provable limits on what users can do *without* the backdoor. That is, the backdoor can be useful even if one can heuristically (but not provably) have more power than anyone else by having access to the backdoor. For example, we would have the flexibility of no longer requiring the model to be bilipschitz after the first layer; lipschitzness itself suffices. This means that we can use standard ReLUs (and variants like GELU) instead of Leaky ReLUs. It also means that we can handle compressing matrices, so we can handle models that have scalar outputs (instead of high-dimensional embeddings). We also would not need to limit ourselves to discrete inputs.

*2.* We expect that DNNs (and other architectures, more broadly) have many computationally hard problems that can be exploited for backdoors. In our work, we focus on the task of finding collisions in a random compressing linear map, but there undoubtedly exist other relevant tasks that no efficient algorithm can feasibly solve. For example, perhaps there is some sense in which finding adversarial examples within transformers can be phrased as a hard computational problem.

**Our notion of backdoors**:

You are right that our notion of a backdoor is dual to the more commonly studied variant which aims to find “expanding” adversarial examples in models instead of collisions. We really think of them as dual notions, with neither being inherently more “reasonable” than the other. The reason we focus on collisions is that finding discrete shrinking vectors in random compressing linear maps is computationally very difficult, as shown in Bogdanov et al. (2025). This is what gives us our backdoor strength. For the dual question of “expanding” vectors in random linear maps, this is not the case: rounding the top singular vector is an efficient algorithm that gives a very close approximation to the true, maximally expanding discrete vector.

Here, we present a scenario in which the “collision” backdoor notion we construct is significant and potentially worrisome. Imagine that one trains a DNN as an image embedding model used within a facial recognition system. Let $M$ denote the model given as a DNN. To recognize a new image $\mathbf{x}$, one would evaluate $M(\mathbf{x})$ and compute the distances between $M(\mathbf{x})$ and $M(\mathbf{x}’)$ for target images $\mathbf{x}’$ and apply a threshold. If there is an existing target image $\mathbf{x}’$ such that $\| M(\mathbf{x}) - M(\mathbf{x}’) \|$ is sufficiently small, there is a “match” and the system recognizes the image.

Our backdoor notion in this setting would mean the following. With the backdoor, one can take any image and generate a fake, different image that is a “fake match” (i.e., false positive) with the original image according to this recognition system. Conversely, without the backdoor, no one else has this ability to “fool” the recognition system in this way, even for one image. If one adopts the more studied notion of backdoors here for “expanding” examples, one would create *false negatives* instead of false positives.

display_title: Official Review of Submission20344 by Reviewer yk7U

summary.value:
This mostly theoretical paper's goal is to prove that it is possible (under cryptographic & other assumptions) to train a neural network in such a way that
- there is a vector $z$ known to the trainer such that adding $z$ to any input $x$ results in an input $x+z$ where the final layer embedding (and in fact any layer embedding) of $x+z$ is very close to that of $x$. 
- for someone with white-box access, it is
	1. statistically infeasible to tell that the training process was "tampered with"
	2. computationally infeasible (w.r.t cryptographic assumptions and polynomial-time complexity) to compute any pair of inputs $(x, x')$ that result in nearly as close final-layer embeddings ("collisions") as for $(x, x+z)$. 

	This is proposed as a way to "backdoor" the model. The proof makes some assumptions on the neural network (importantly, bi-Lipschitzness of the composition of layers after the 1st), which essentially reduce it to showing that the 1st layer can be set up to have the main property we want. The proof heavily relies on the prior work [1], which shows among other things that finding collisions in a matrix $A$ drawn from a certain random ensemble is computationally intractable. This random ensemble is used as a basis for the construction, which proceeds by first choosing ~any $z$, and then rejection sampling the rows of $A$ so that they ensure $z$ has the collision property. The main difficulty in the paper is to show that the rejection sampling does not move the distribution of the matrix $A$ too much away from the random ensemble the result in [1] is based on. This also ensures the statistical infeasibility of distinguishing the trained network from a "normally" trained one. 
	
[1] Andrej Bogdanov, Alon Rosen, Neekon Vafa, and Vinod Vaikuntanathan. Adaptive robustness of hypergrid johnson-lindenstrauss.

strengths.value:
- Writing is clear and motivates and describes the math well, providing useful intuition and context in prior work
- Strong results on infeasibility to know that the training process was modified, and to be able to produce collisions without the hidden attacker vector $z$
- Some empirical validation

weaknesses.value:
- The core of the result and all the work happens in the first layer of the network; the bi-Lipschitzness assumption quite easily takes care of the rest of the network. As such, it's a major assumption, and it's uncler the extent to which we can expect it to hold in practice. For instance, the existence of adversarial examples suggests that bi-Lipschitzness can't be too strong
- There is important reliance in the result on the degree of compression happening in the first layer. It's important to note that modern practical neural networks do not have arbitrarily high compression ratios; 1/10 seems a reasonable lower bound.
- it's unclear why this should be considered a "backdoor". I don't see a practically relevant scenario where an attacker could derive some benefit from the existence of these collisions.

questions.value:
- why should we be worried about backdoors like that? to me it seems much more natural to use this as a watermarking tool.
- in practice, how bad is the breakdown in the bi-Lipschitz property due to adversarial examples

comment.value:
Thank you for your positive review. We’re glad that you appreciated our clear writing and strong infeasibility results. We respond to your review below, and we hope that our response adequately addresses your questions and concerns. If not, please let us know so that we can appropriately respond. We have also uploaded a **revision** of our paper that includes a new section addressing your comment on watermarking; see Section 1.2 in the revision.

**Lipschitzness and adversarial examples**:

As you correctly point out, bilipschitzness and the existence of adversarial examples are intrinsically related; a function’s bilipschitz constants exactly determine the extent to which sensitivity-based (“expanding”) or invariance-based (“colliding”) adversarial examples exist in the function. Indeed, lots of empirical works have exploited lack of bilipschitzness to produce adversarial examples. In our experiments, as has been observed previously in the literature, we noticed that the final layer of a DNN was particularly ill-conditioned after training.

Given that bilipschitzness and adversarial examples are inherently connected, a natural approach to prevent adversarial examples is to deliberately enforce lipschitzness during training (e.g., Maas et al. (2013); Cissé et al. (2017); Yoshida & Miyato (2017); Jia et al. (2017); Bansal et al. (2018); Miyato et al. (2018); Huang et al. (2018); Pauli et al. (2022); Ducotterd et al. (2024)). One interpretation of our work is that enforcing bilipschitzness in almost every layer of a DNN (i.e., everywhere except the first layer) is insufficient to prevent adversarial examples; even making the first layer a compressing random matrix is already enough to generate strong invariance-based adversarial examples, even if the rest of the model is bilipschitz.

**Use of our backdoors**:

Below, we present a scenario in which the backdoor notion we construct is significant and potentially worrisome. Imagine that one trains a DNN as an image embedding model used within a facial recognition system. Let $M$ denote the model given as a DNN. To recognize a new image $\mathbf{x}$, one would evaluate $M(\mathbf{x})$ and compute the distances between $M(\mathbf{x})$ and $M(\mathbf{x}’)$ for target images $\mathbf{x}’$ and apply a threshold. If there is an existing target image $\mathbf{x}’$ such that $\| M(\mathbf{x}) - M(\mathbf{x}’) \|$ is sufficiently small, there is a “match” and the system recognizes the image.

Our backdoor notion in this setting would mean the following. With the backdoor, one can take any image and generate a fake, different image that is a “fake match” with the original image according to this recognition system. Conversely, without the backdoor, no one else has this ability to “fool” the recognition system, even for one image.

We thank you for bringing up the notion of watermarking. In the introduction, we briefly mentioned a “positive use” of our backdoors, which could be used as an authentication mechanism to establish model provenance / ownership. Indeed, this directly follows from our backdoor definition; any colliding adversarial example directly proves “ownership”, in the sense of proof of sampling the matrix $\mathbf{A}$. In our revision, Section 1.2 elaborates on this point, but if there are any particular questions about this application that you have, please let us know.

**Compression Ratios**:

We agree that the quantitative bounds in our result depend significantly on the compression ratio of the first layer. Table 1 shows that compression ratios of 1/10, 2/10, and 3/10 plausibly all have large backdoor strength, with room to spare. Therefore, even if modern neural networks have a compression ratio lower bound of 1/10, our result is still meaningful.

display_title: Meta Review of Submission20344 by Area Chair r6LG

reviewer_concerns.value:
Concerns addressed by the rebuttal:

(1) The authors clarified the motivation and interpretation of their backdoor notion, explaining why invariance-based (collision) backdoors are meaningful and how they relate to alternative views such as model provenance / watermarking.
(2) Questions regarding why this notion differs from standard “expanding” adversarial examples were addressed with a clearer justification of the cryptographic hardness underlying collision-based constructions.
(3) Several reviewers’ requests for clarification on the threat model, training randomness, and the relationship to prior work (e.g., JL embeddings and collision hardness) were reasonably answered, improving conceptual clarity.

Concerns that remain outstanding:

(1) The results still rely on strong and restrictive architectural assumptions, especially the frozen compressing first layer and bi-Lipschitz constraints, leaving open how far the theory extends to modern, unconstrained DNNs.
(2)The practical security relevance of the proposed backdoors remains debatable; some reviewers remain unconvinced that the constructed collisions correspond to realistic or harmful backdoor behavior in deployed systems.
(3) Questions about real-world stealthiness and applicability, including whether the unusual architecture itself could raise suspicion and how the attack would manifest in practical settings, are only partially addressed.

Overall, the rebuttal improves exposition and positioning, but concerns about generality and practical impact remain.
